questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy with a prior diagnosis of Tourette’s disorder is referred to your care. His mother tells you that during middle school he was teased for having vocal and motor tics. Since starting ninth grade, his tics have become less frequent. Currently, only mild motor tics remain. What is the appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: Persistent (chronic) motor tic disorder is present with these symptoms.
A diagnosis of provisional tic disorder.
A diagnosis of unspecified tic disorder.
Persistent (chronic) vocal tic disorder describes her presentation.

questions.explanation: There are four tic disorder diagnostic categories, and they follow a hierarchical order: 1) Tourette’s disorder, 2) persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder, 3) provisional tic disorder, and 4) unspecified tic disorder. According to Criterion E for tic disorders in DSM-5, once someone is diagnosed with a tic disorder at one level of the hierarchy, a diagnosis that is lower in the hierarchy cannot be made. In this case, option A is the correct answer because the boy has already been previously diagnosed with Tourette’s disorder, which is at the top of the tic disorder hierarchy. Thus, at this point, he can no longer be diagnosed with persistent (chronic) motor tic disorder (option B). Options C and D are incorrect.

questions.question_text: Rocking, head-banging, and self-mutilation are recognised signs of which form of child maltreatment?
questions.explanation: The source lists under Signs of possible emotional abuse: Low self-esteem, continual self-deprecation, Sudden speech disorder, Rocking, head-banging, or other neurotic behaviour, and Self-mutilation. These neurotic and self-harming behaviours are characteristic of emotional abuse. The other forms have different presentations.

questions.question_text: Physical abuse is highly associated with which psychosocial factor?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that although child abuse occurs at all socioeconomic levels, it is highly associated with poverty and psychosocial stress, especially financial stress.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements most accurately characterizes the development of childhood-onset fluency disorder (stuttering)?

options.text: The typical age of onset is 2–7 years, with 80–90% of affected individuals showing onset by age 6
Stuttering affects males and females equally in prevalence
Emotional stress and anxiety have no influence on the severity of stuttering
Stuttering is caused exclusively by learned behaviour with no genetic contribution
Motor movements such as eye blinks and facial grimacing are never observed in association with stuttering

correct_answer.text: The typical age of onset is 2–7 years, with 80–90% of affected individuals showing onset by age 6

questions.explanation: Childhood-onset fluency disorder (stuttering) typically begins between ages 2 and 7 years, with 80–90% of affected individuals showing onset by age 6 (Kaplan & Sadock p.2450; MRCPsych Notes p.96). It affects males approximately three times more frequently than females. Emotional stress and anxiety can exacerbate stuttering, though they are not its sole cause — aetiology is multifactorial, including genetic and neurophysiological factors. Associated motor movements such as eye blinks, facial grimaces, and head jerks may accompany disrupted speech.

questions.question_text: A five-year-old child who was abused and neglected runs to a social worker, sits on their knee, and readily asks to go home with them. Which disorder does this behavior suggest?
questions.explanation: Disinhibited social engagement disorder is characterized by grossly abnormal social behaviour in the context of inadequate care. The child approaches adults indiscriminately, lacks reticence to approach, will go away with unfamiliar adults, and exhibits overly familiar behaviour towards strangers.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which best defi nes the diagnosis of specifi c reading disorder when assessed using psychometric measures of reading age?

options.text: Reading age is below the 10th percentile of the peers
Reading age is one standard deviation below the expected
Reading age is two standard deviations below the expected
Reading age is three standard deviations below the expected
Reading age is below the 20th percentile of the peers

correct_answer.text: Reading age is two standard deviations below the expected

questions.explanation: According to current classifi catory systems, a learning disorder such as specifi c reading disorder can be diagnosed when the child achieves substantially lower than expected scores on individually administered, standardized tests of components of learning (reading, mathematics, or written expression) for a given age, schooling, and level of intelligence. Thus an explicit reference to psychometric assessments is made when diagnosing learning disorders. But a specifi c guideline as to the statistical meaning of being substantially below the expected norm is not clearly delineated in DSM IV. Nevertheless, ICD-10 states a score that is at least 2 standard errors of prediction below the expected value as diagnostic criteria for specifi c developmental disorders of scholastic skills. Gelder MG, et al., eds. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 667.

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old girl presents with nightmares, sleep disturbances, running away from home, and reluctance to be alone. Which form of abuse should be highest in the differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of sleep disturbances, running away, fear of sleeping alone, and withdrawal are listed as behavioral signs of possible sexual abuse. The presentation is more consistent with trauma response than other forms of abuse.

questions.question_text: A child psychiatrist evaluates an 8-year-old with social difficulties to differentiate ADHD from autism spectrum disorder. Which feature most strongly suggests autism rather than ADHD?
questions.explanation: Impaired social cognition and not understanding social cues is a core feature of autism spectrum disorder.

questions.question_text: Which psychiatric outcome is associated with childhood adversities across the lifespan in the WHO World Mental Health Survey?
questions.explanation: That the association between childhood adversities and first onset of a wide variety of mental disorders across the life course found consistent global effects for all major DSM-IV disorders.

questions.question_text: What is the female-to-male ratio of victims in childhood sexual abuse?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that girls are more often the victims at a 4:1 ratio.

questions.question_text: A 5yearold child is brought to the clinic by his mother for “not being like other children” at home and school. You find that the child does not make appropriate eye contact with others, including his mother, and also fails to respond to the social cues put forth by his mother. Reports from school describe a lack of the ability for spontaneous makebelieve play and a delay in language development. Although there are various toys in the office, the child is fixated on playing with a shiny candy bar wrapper that was in the trash bin. His mother reports that some of these symptoms have been present from around the age of 3, but she thought “he’d grow out of it.” What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder
A diagnosis of avoidant personality disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder

questions.explanation: This presentation is diagnostic of autism spectrum disorder. Patients with autism have deficient social skills such as a lack of the ability to read or use nonverbal gestures or an inability to engage in emotional reciprocity. They demonstrate communication deficits such as delays in language development or repetitive or idiosyncratic use of language. They do not engage in makebelieve play. They also exhibit repetitive or stereotypical patterns of behaviors such as abnormal, persistent preoccupation with areas of interest or parts of objects. Some of the symptoms must be present prior to age 3 years. Y BoARd RevIew

questions.question_text: A clinician notes that a child with emotional abuse history demonstrates low self-esteem and sudden onset of stuttering. Which neurological process might explain the speech disorder?
questions.explanation: Sudden speech disorder is listed as a sign of emotional abuse, suggesting that psychological stress from abuse disrupts established speech patterns rather than affecting primary language development, distinguishing this from developmental language disorders.

questions.question_text: The effects of maternal depression on infant development include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Conduct disorders are listed as consequences in school-age children and adolescents, not infants. Infants typically display anger, protective coping, passivity, withdrawal, reduced attention, and lower IQ.

questions.question_text: Which Rutter-outlined mediator of parental psychiatric disorder's effect on a child refers to genetic or constitutional factors?
questions.explanation: Rutter identified three categories: direct pernicious impact, indirect impact via altered parenting, and mediator variables (which include social adversity, genetic or constitutional factors).

correct_answer.text: Repeated messaging that the child is worthless, defective, or unwanted

Sexual behaviour between a child and an adult involving coercion
Failure to provide adequate care and protection, including withholding physical, emotional, and educational necessities
Repeated conveyance that a child is worthless or unwanted
Inducing illness in a child to obtain medical attention

correct_answer.text: Failure to provide adequate care and protection, including withholding physical, emotional, and educational necessities

questions.explanation: Neglect as the most prevalent form of child maltreatment involving failure to provide adequate care and protection, with malicious or ignorant withholding of physical, emotional, and educational necessities. Option D describes emotional abuse, E describes factitious disorder by proxy, A describes physical abuse, and B describes sexual abuse.

questions.question_text: All of the below options apply are recognized associations with specifi c reading disorder with the exception of

options.text: Difficulty in visual scanning and tracking
Natural remission with development and maturation
Increased incidence among children with seizure disorders

questions.explanation: Deterioration of already acquired language skills is not seen in specifi c reading disorder or dyslexia. Neurodevelopmental basis for dyslexia is suggested by the similarity of certain symptoms in dyslexic children and the neurological syndrome of `visual word blindness’ that results from damage to the left inferior parieto-occipital region (more specifi cally, the left angular gyrus). This region is speculated to have a role in processing the optic images of letters; damage to this region may lead to defects in visual scanning. It is also noted that dyslexic children have poor or delayed brain lateralization, especially for language. The high incidence of left-handers, right-left confusion and the mirror-writing phenomenon noted in dyslexia can be considered as indirect support to this notion. Epileptic children may have higher incidence of dyslexia. General improvement with age suggests a brain maturational delay in the aetiology of dyslexia. Gelder MG, et al., eds. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 669. Habib M. The neurological basis of developmental dyslexia: an overview and working hypothesis. Brain 2000; 123: 2373–2399.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes developmental coordination disorder (DCD)?

options.text: Some children with DCD show additional (commonly suppressed) motor activity, such as choreiform movements of unsupported limbs or mirror movements.
The prevalence of developmental coordination disorder in children ages 5-11 is approximately 1-3%.
In early adulthood, there is improvement in learning new tasks involving complex/automatic motor skills, encompassing driving and using tools.
Developmental coordination disorder has no association with prenatal alcohol exposure or birth weight.
Neurodevelopmental processes are not impaired in developmental coordination disorder.

correct_answer.text: Some children with DCD show additional (commonly suppressed) motor activity, such as choreiform movements of unsupported limbs or mirror movements.

questions.explanation: In regard to the choreiform or mirror movements seen in DCD, DSM-5 states, “these ‘overflow’ movements are referred to as neurodevelopmental immaturities or neurological soft signs rather than neurological abnormalities. In both current literature and clinical practice, their role in diagnosis is still unclear, requiring further evaluation.” The prevalence of DCD in children ages 5– 11 years is 5%–6% (in children age 7 years, 1.8% are diagnosed with severe DCD and 3% with probable DCD). In adulthood, there are often ongoing problems with learning new tasks involving complex/automatic motor skills. DCD is more common following prenatal exposure to alcohol and in preterm and low-birth-weight children. In DCD, deficits have been identified in both visuomotor perception and spatial mentalizing; these deficits affect the ability to make rapid motoric adjustments as the complexity of the required movements increases.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which fails to qualify as a criterion for the DSM-5 diagnosis of attentiondeficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?

options.text: Onset must occur before age 6 years for ADHD to be diagnosed.
Symptoms must be evident in at least one setting such as school.
Persistence of symptoms for at least 12 months.
Symptoms must persist for at least 6 months before diagnosis.
Symptoms must cause clinically significant impairment in social or academic functioning.

correct_answer.text: Persistence of symptoms for at least 12 months.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of ADHD is a pervasive pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development, with persistence of symptoms for at least 6 months to a degree that is inconsistent with developmental level and that negatively impacts directly on social and academic/occupational activities. ADHD begins in childhood. The requirement that several symptoms be present before age 12 years conveys the importance of a substantial clinical presentation during childhood. Manifestations of the disorder must be present in more than one setting (e.g., home and school, work). Confirmation of substantial symptoms across settings typically cannot be done accurately without consulting informants who have seen the individual in those settings.

When parents had primary identity tied only to parenting
In families where both parents work

questions.question_text: An 18-month-old child in a care institution does not seek comfort from caregivers when injured. Which attachment disorder is this consistent with?
questions.explanation: Reactive attachment disorder is characterized by grossly abnormal attachment behaviours in early childhood in the context of inadequate care. The child does not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort and rarely displays security-seeking behaviours toward any adult.

questions.question_text: In order for a child to meet criteria for a diagnosis of gender dysphoria, which of the following must be present?

options.text: A co-occurring disorder of sex development.
A strong desire to be of the other gender or an insistence that one is the other gender.
A strong dislike of one’s sexual anatomy.
A stated wish to change gender.
A strong desire for the primary and/or secondary sex characteristics that match one’s experienced gender.

correct_answer.text: A strong desire to be of the other gender or an insistence that one is the other gender.

questions.explanation: For a child to meet criteria for a gender dysphoria diagnosis, there must be a strong desire to be the other gender or an insistence that one is the other gender (Criterion A1). The inclusion of this criterion in DSM-5 makes the diagnosis more conservative. The strong desire need not be stated aloud, because DSM-5 recognizes that social and/or cultural factors may inhibit this expression. There may be a strong dislike of one’s sexual anatomy, or a strong desire for sex characteristics that match one’s experienced gender, but these are not necessary for the diagnosis. There may be a co-occurring disorder of sex development, but this is not necessary for the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Considered to be the new developmental phase of the 21st century, this phase, characterised by a tendency for early adults to delay achievements, has been coined:
questions.explanation: Emerging adulthood is the phase following late adolescence that was officially named by James Arnett in 2000. It is still unclear whether this is a new developmental phase or a phenomenon due to current societal values. questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes development of and risk factors for intellectual disability (intellectual developmental disorder)?

options.text: Intellectual developmental disorder cannot be diagnosed when a known genetic syndrome is present.
Etiologies are limited to postnatal factors occurring after early infancy.
In severe acquired forms of intellectual developmental disorder, onset may be abrupt following an illness (e.g., meningitis) or head trauma occurring during the developmental phase.
Only the acquired intellectual disability diagnosis is assigned when disability results from trauma.
Prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal etiologies of intellectual developmental disorder are demonstrable in roughly 33% of cases.

correct_answer.text: In severe acquired forms of intellectual developmental disorder, onset may be abrupt following an illness (e.g., meningitis) or head trauma occurring during the developmental phase.

questions.explanation: The presence of a known genetic syndrome is not exclusionary if the criteria for intellectual developmental disorder are met. Prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal etiologies are demonstrable in approximately 70% of cases. If the diagnosis results from TBI, both diagnoses are given.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes childhood-onset schizophrenia?

options.text: Childhood-onset schizophrenia tends to resemble poor-outcome adult schizophrenia, with gradual onset and prominent negative symptoms.
Disorganized speech patterns in childhood are commonly indicative of schizophrenia.
Because of the childhood capacity for imagination, delusions and hallucinations in childhood-onset schizophrenia are more elaborate than those in adult-onset schizophrenia.
Catatonia would be appropriate if muscle tension patterns were evident.
Visual hallucinations are extremely rare in childhood-onset schizophrenia.

correct_answer.text: Childhood-onset schizophrenia tends to resemble poor-outcome adult schizophrenia, with gradual onset and prominent negative symptoms.

questions.explanation: The essential features of schizophrenia are the same in childhood, but it is more difficult to make the diagnosis. In children, delusions and hallucinations may be less elaborate than in adults, and visual hallucinations are more common and should be distinguished from normal fantasy play. Disorganized speech occurs in many disorders with childhood onset (e.g., autism spectrum disorder), as does disorganized behavior (e.g., attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder). These symptoms should not be attributed to schizophrenia without due consideration of the more common disorders of childhood. Childhood-onset cases tend to resemble poor-outcome adult cases, with gradual onset and prominent negative symptoms. Children who later receive the diagnosis of schizophrenia are more likely to have experienced nonspecific emotional-behavioral disturbances and psychopathology, intellectual and language alterations, and subtle motor delays.

questions.question_text: The diagnostic criteria for oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) encompasses specifiers for indicating severity of the disorder as manifested by pervasiveness of symptoms across settings and relationships. which of the following options specifiers would be appropriate for an 11-year-old boy who meets Criterion A symptoms in two settings?

options.text: A diagnosis of mild with less than 4 symptoms.
A diagnosis of severe with 8 or more symptoms.
A diagnosis of extreme with all symptoms present.
There is not enough information to code the specifier.

questions.explanation: The “mild” specifier requires symptoms to be confined to one setting, the “moderate” specifier requires symptoms to be present in at least two settings, and the “severe” specifier requires symptoms to be present in at least three settings. There is no “extreme” specifier.

questions.question_text: A toddler with maternal depression shows reduced cooperative play and social interaction. Which developmental consequence is this child at highest risk for manifesting in school age?

options.text: Reduced adaptive functioning and affective/anxiety disorders

correct_answer.text: Reduced adaptive functioning and affective/anxiety disorders

questions.question_text: A toddler exhibits no cooperative play and reduced social interaction following exposure to maternal depression. This outcome is BEST explained by which mediating mechanism?

options.text: Direct exposure to maternal mood symptoms creating environmental unpredictability
Altered parenting capacity reducing scaffolding of social skills

correct_answer.text: Altered parenting capacity reducing scaffolding of social skills

questions.explanation: The toddler's reduced social interaction and absent cooperative play reflect inadequate parental scaffolding and modelling—direct consequences of altered parenting capacity (Rutter's second mediator). Genetic vulnerability (A) and prenatal effects (E) would not specifically cause this. Direct mood exposure (B) and poverty alone (D) are less direct mechanisms.

questions.question_text: An unexplained injury with an improbable excuse in a child should raise suspicion for which form of maltreatment?

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes the onset and developmental course of conduct disorder?

options.text: Onset may occur as early as the preschool years and is rare after age 16years.
Onset typically occurs in middle adolescence.
Age at onset has no bearing on the developmental course of the disorder.
Oppositional defiant disorder is generally not a precursor to the childhoodonset type of conduct disorder.
Those with adolescent-onset type typically have worse adjustment as adults.

correct_answer.text: Onset may occur as early as the preschool years and is rare after age 16years.

questions.explanation: The onset of conduct disorder typically occurs in the period from middle childhood through middle adolescence, although symptoms may appear in the preschool years. Individuals with adolescent-onset type and those with fewer and milder symptoms tend to have a greater likelihood of being successful (from a social and occupational standpoint) as adults. Oppositional defiant disorder is a common precursor to the childhood-onset type of conduct disorder.

Constant hunger, poor hygiene, and untreated medical problems WITHOUT injury

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old boy has difficulty making friends and problems with initiating and sustaining back-and-forth conversation; reading social cues; and sharing his feelings with others. He makes good eye contact, has normal speech intonation, demonstrates facial gestures, and has a range of affect that generally seems appropriate to the situation. He demonstrates an interest in trains that seems abnormal in intensity and focus, and he engages in little imaginative or symbolic play. which of the following options diagnostic requirements for autism spectrum disorder are not met in this case? Neurodevelopmental Disorders—QUESTIONS | 7

options.text: A diagnosis of deficits in social-emotional reciprocity.
Impairment in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction.
Impairment in developing and maintaining relationships.
Restricted patterns must be present in at least three of the four specified behavioral categories.
Autism spectrum disorder requires symptom onset after age 3 years for diagnosis.

correct_answer.text: Impairment in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction.

questions.explanation: DSM-5 Criterion A for autism spectrum disorder specifies that all three symptom clusters (summarized in options A, B, and C above) must be met. This boy’s nonverbal communication is reported to be unimpaired (although this should be confirmed with a standard instrument such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule). Based on the current history, he could not be diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5. In order to meet Criterion B, at least two symptom clusters must be met. Although the boy has “highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus,” he would need to have at least one other symptom from categories in Criterion B (which includes stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech; insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns of verbal or nonverbal behavior; or hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment).

questions.question_text: A 5-year-old girl is referred to your care with a DSM-IV diagnosis of chronic motor or vocal tic disorder. Under DSM-5, she would meet criteria for persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder. which of the following options statements about her new diagnosis under DSM-5 is inaccurate?

options.text: She can have either motor or vocal tics, but not both types simultaneously.
Her tics must persist for more than 1 year since first tic onset without a ticfree period for 3 consecutive months to meet diagnostic criteria. Neurodevelopmental Disorders—QUESTIONS | 19
Tics may fluctuate in frequency while persisting beyond 1 year.
She has never experienced symptoms that would meet Tourette's disorder criteria.
Diagnostic specifiers include information about associated medical conditions.

correct_answer.text: Her tics must persist for more than 1 year since first tic onset without a ticfree period for 3 consecutive months to meet diagnostic criteria. Neurodevelopmental Disorders—QUESTIONS | 19

questions.explanation: Under DSM-5 criteria for persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder, tics may wax and wane. There is also no longer a requirement for a tic-free period. Thus, option C is true, and option B is the false statement. Options A and D are diagnostic criteria that are true for this classification under both DSM-IV and DSM-5. Option E is true because in DSM-5, one can specify “motor tics only” or “vocal tics only.”

questions.question_text: Physical abuse most commonly begins at which developmental period?

questions.question_text: A 4-month-old male child is brought to a paediatrician because he is not ingesting enough milk and is underweight for his age. Nutritional supplementation in addition to breastfeeding is recommended. The child is distressed and vomits when feeding on these supplements. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluating this child?

options.text: Reassure the parents that vomiting after supplemental feeding is normal at this age and no further evaluation is needed
Commence empirical proton pump inhibitor therapy without further investigation
Recommend evaluation for functional or structural GI disorder
Refer the child to a lactation consultant only, as vomiting is likely due to breastfeeding technique

correct_answer.text: Recommend evaluation for functional or structural GI disorder

questions.explanation: In a 4-month-old presenting with poor weight gain, feeding distress, and vomiting on supplemental feeds, the priority is to evaluate for an underlying functional or structural gastrointestinal disorder. Conditions such as gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), pyloric stenosis, cow\'s milk protein allergy, and other structural anomalies must be considered and appropriately investigated before attributing symptoms to feeding technique alone. Simply reassuring parents (A) or commencing empirical treatment without investigation (B) risks missing a treatable structural diagnosis. A lactation review alone (D) would not address the distress and vomiting that occur with non-breastmilk supplemental feeds, suggesting the problem is not solely breastfeeding-related.

questions.question_text: Which psychiatric outcome is specifically mentioned as a consequence of maternal depression in adolescents but NOT in school-age children?
questions.explanation: Substance abuse and alcohol dependence are listed only in the adolescent section. School-age children show reduced adaptive functioning, affective/anxiety/conduct disorders, and ADHD-like presentations, but substance abuse is not mentioned.

Individuals with ADHD show better occupational performance and attendance than peers.

Individuals with characteristics described in this specifier may be more likely than other individuals with conduct disorder to engage in aggression that is planned for instrumental gain. questions.question_text: Among the following, which is a characteristic feature of paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder due to group A streptococcal infection (PANDAS)?

In fact, Levinson says that it is not a diagnosis, but a syndrome where obsessive compulsive disorder and tics have been exacerbated in children following a group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) infection. The diagnostic criteria for PANDAS that were proposed by Swedo et al. in 1998 include the following: OCD and/or chronic tic disorder (Tourette’s, chronic motor, or vocal tic disorder) that meets the DSM-IV diagnostic criteria; age at onset between 3 years and the onset of puberty; clinical course with an abrupt onset of symptoms and/or a pattern of dramatic recurrent exacerbations and remissions; temporal relation between GABHS infection and onset and/or exacerbations of clinical symptoms; and neurologic abnormalities such as motoric hyperactivity, tics, or choreiform activity during an exacerbation. questions.question_text: A 15yearold male is brought to the emergency room by ambulance for an acute change in behavior. questions.question_text: How are stereotypies differentiated from tics?

options.text: Stereotypies tend to be unilateral; tics tend to be bilateral.
Stereotypies have an earlier onset than tics.
Stereotypy intensity tends to fluctuate; tics tend to be consistent over time.
Stereotypies have a later onset than tics.

correct_answer.text: Stereotypies have an earlier onset than tics.

questions.explanation: Stereotypies and tics are easily confused. Stereotypies usually tend to have an earlier age of onset than do tics (usually at around 2 or 3 years of age), are bilateral, and are consistent throughout time as opposed to the fluctuating patterns of tics.

questions.question_text: According to the source, childhood adversities associated with which type of family functioning elevate the risk of adult psychiatric disorders most significantly?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that adversities associated with maladaptive family functioning elevate the risk of adult psychiatric disorders (all major DSM-IV disorders) with an odds ratio of 1.3–2.4.

questions.question_text: Among the options below, which one is not typically an effective and recommended method of treating enuresis in childhood?
questions.explanation: Enuresis should first be treated with behavioral conditioning (such as bellandpad conditioning) treatments prior to pharmacological modalities. If symptoms persist, medications such as desmopressin (DDAVP) and TCAs such as amitriptyline and imipramine may be effective. Antipsychotics such as risperidone do not play a role in the treatment of childhood enuresis.

questions.question_text: What is the most common childhood adversity identified in the WHO World Mental Health Survey Initiative across 21 countries?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that parental death is the most common childhood adversity at 11.0–14.8%, whereas physical abuse is 5.3–10.8%, family violence 4.2–7.8%, and parental mental illness 5.3–6.7%.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old shows poor growth, weight loss, and poor skin tone without organic cause. Which form of maltreatment does this presentation MOST strongly indicate?

options.text: Physical neglect and non-organic failure to thrive

correct_answer.text: Physical neglect and non-organic failure to thrive

questions.explanation: The source lists significant lack of growth, weight loss, poor skin tone, and muscle tone as signs of possible non-organic failure to thrive, which is grouped with neglect signs. This presentation without organic cause indicates inadequate nutrition and care provision (neglect).

questions.question_text: A toddler with a history of maternal depression is most likely to exhibit which behavioral pattern?

options.text: Passive noncompliance and reduced autonomy expression

correct_answer.text: Passive noncompliance and reduced autonomy expression

questions.explanation: The source lists effects on toddlers as passive noncompliance, reduced expression of autonomy, internalizing and externalizing problems, and reduced social interaction.

questions.question_text: What is the gender ratio of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children?

options.text: A diagnosis of male:female ratio of 2:1.
A diagnosis of male:female ratio of 3:2.
A diagnosis of male:female ratio of 5:1.
A diagnosis of male:female ratio of 1:2.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of male:female ratio of 2:1.

questions.explanation: ADHD is more prevalent in males than in females in the general population, with a gender ratio of approximately 2:1 in children and 1.6:1 in adults. Females are more likely than males to present primarily with inattentive features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a physical sign of possible sexual abuse in a child?
questions.explanation: Recurrent vaginal infection, discharge, and unexplained bleeding are listed as physical/medical signs of possible sexual abuse. The other options are signs of neglect or general abuse.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is considered a normative crisis?
questions.explanation: Normative crises are periods of change that stretch a person’s adaptive capabilities. A midlife crisis is a type of normative crisis. A midlife crisis is considered a critical point in a person’s life associated with emotional instability involving alterations in major commitments (e.g., career or marriage). Marriage and graduation are considered rites of passage.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is not a symptom for the diagnosis of oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) in DSM5?
questions.explanation: The three classes of symptoms outlined in the DSM5 criteria for ODD include vindictiveness, angry/ irritable mood, and argumentative/ defiant behavior. questions.question_text: Among the following options, which was a criterion symptom for autistic disorder in DSMIV that was eliminated from the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5?

options.text: Inability to maintain appropriate eye contact during conversation.
Speech delay without language comprehension difficulties.
A diagnosis of inflexible adherence to routines.
Persistent preoccupation with parts of objects.
Failure to respond to nonverbal bids for joint attention from others.

correct_answer.text: Persistent preoccupation with parts of objects.

questions.explanation: In DSM-5, the older requirement regarding objects was restated as follows: “Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g., strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interests)” in Criterion B3. In Criterion B4, DSM-5 mentions “fascination with lights or spinning objects.” There is no mention of preoccupation with “parts of objects” in DSM-5 (Criterion A3d in DSM-IV autistic disorder).

questions.question_text: A 7-year-old boy with a history of maternal depression presents with reduced ability to adapt to school demands and emerging affective symptoms. This progression best exemplifies which consequence pattern?
questions.explanation: The progression from toddler symptoms (passive noncompliance, reduced autonomy) to school-age symptoms (reduced adaptive functioning, affective symptoms) illustrates the developmental trajectory outlined in the source.

questions.question_text: According to the source, which consequence appears specifically in adolescents exposed to maternal depression but not in younger developmental stages?
questions.explanation: Substance abuse and alcohol dependence are listed specifically under adolescent consequences of maternal depression, not in earlier developmental stages (infants, toddlers, school-age children).

questions.question_text: Which factor serves as a protective factor in childhood development?
questions.explanation: A sensitive, responsive mother who provides emotional support and attunement is a significant protective factor in childhood development.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which fails to qualify as representative of the typical developmental course for autism spectrum disorder?

options.text: A diagnosis of lack of degenerative course.
A diagnosis of behavioral deterioration during adolescence.
Individuals with autism typically have continued cognitive decline throughout life.
Behavioral deterioration and loss of skills typically occur during adolescence.
Most individuals with autism spectrum disorder experience significant unemployment and require full-time care.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of behavioral deterioration during adolescence.

questions.explanation: Most adolescents with autism spectrum disorder improve behaviorally; only a minority further deteriorates.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy has a long prior diagnosis of nonverbal communication deficits. As an infant he was unable to follow someone else directing his attention by pointing. As a toddler he was not interested in sharing events, feelings, or games with his parents. From school age into adolescence, his speech was odd in tonality and phrasing, and his body language was awkward. What do these symptoms represent?

options.text: A diagnosis of restricted range of interests.
A diagnosis of prodromal schizophreniform symptoms.

questions.explanation: These symptoms are examples of deficits in nonverbal communicative behavior, as described in Criterion A2 for autism spectrum disorder criteria in DSM-5.

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old child presents with depressive symptoms, anxiety, and conduct problems following documented parental psychiatric illness. Which developmental stage consequence from maternal depression does this clinical presentation BEST match?
questions.explanation: School-age children show reduced adaptive functioning, affective, anxiety, and conduct disorders, plus ADHD-like presentations. This triad of depression, anxiety, and conduct problems matches school-age consequences exactly, not adolescent (which adds substance abuse) or other stages.

questions.question_text: A child with ADHD and liver disease has not responded to stimulant medication and parents don't want a sedating medication. Which medication is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Guanfacine is an alpha-2 agonist that is less sedating than clonidine and does not require hepatic metabolism like atomoxetine, making it suitable for liver disease.

questions.question_text: A 12-year-old with school-age consequences of maternal depression shows reduced adaptive functioning and ADHD-like presentations. Which intervention approach would MOST directly target the identified mediating mechanism according to Rutter's framework?

options.text: Genetic counselling for the child's future reproductive risk
Improving the mother's depression treatment and parenting capacity (targeting altered parenting as mediator)
Environmental enrichment programs unrelated to parental involvement
Separating the child from the mother immediately
Addressing only the child's ADHD symptoms pharmacologically

correct_answer.text: Improving the mother's depression treatment and parenting capacity (targeting altered parenting as mediator)

questions.explanation: The source identifies altered parenting capacity as a key mediator. Improving maternal depression treatment and parenting directly addresses this mechanism (Rutter's second mediator), potentially improving the child's adaptive functioning. Options A, C, D, and E bypass or don't target the primary mediating pathway.

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old boy has a long history of defiant behavior toward authority figures. Recently, he has escalated to aggression toward peers (getting into physical fights at school), destruction of property (punching holes in walls), lying, and stealing money and jewelry from his parents. He does not seem pervasively irritable or depressed, and he has no psychotic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This boy displays aggression toward people, destruction of property, and deceitfulness or theft—all part of Criterion A for conduct disorder in DSM-5. Individuals with Oppositional Defiant Disorder are not typically aggressive toward people or animals and do not generally destroy property.

questions.question_text: A 14yearold female child has difficulty socializing with friends. Her mother reports that her daughter has a very difficult time visiting her friends’ homes, and while she is there she often calls home to make sure her mother is fine and will be able to pick her up. One week ago she went to a friend’s home and began sweating, shaking, crying, and vomiting. She could not be comforted until she was brought back home. Her mother says that when her daughter was 5, she was very clingy and would hit her mother when she dropped her off at school. The individual does not experience these symptoms when her friends come to her home and while her mother is nearby. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of dependent personality disorder
A diagnosis of oppositional defiant disorder
A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder
A diagnosis of social anxiety disorder
A diagnosis of borderline personality disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: A characteristic feature of separation anxiety disorder is experiencing anxiety in the context of separation from home or attachment figures. Individuals with separation anxiety disorder refuse to go anywhere that would take them away from attachment figures, and some children may get aggressive if forced to separate. They also worry about something happening to themselves or to the attachment figures when they are not together. They often have difficulty sleeping by themselves and away from parents and may experience nightmares of something bad happening to the parents. Physical symptoms like headaches and gastrointestinal discomfort are common. The disturbance must last for a period of at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents younger than 18 years and is typically 6 months or longer in adults. The patient described above is able to socialize well at her home and is anxious only when she separates from her mother, which makes social anxiety disorder less plausible. 218 • PSYCHIATRY ReFeReNCeS American Psychiatric Association. Multiple psychopathological consequences of a single trauma

questions.question_text: In order to be considered a symptom of conduct disorder, running away must have occurred with what frequency?

options.text: A diagnosis of at least twice.
A diagnosis of at least four times.
Only once if the patients did not return for a lengthy period.
Twice, in response to physical or sexual abuse.

correct_answer.text: Only once if the patients did not return for a lengthy period.

questions.explanation: DSM-5 specifies that running away can occur once if it is for a lengthy period, or at least twice otherwise. The running away cannot be in response to physical or sexual abuse.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy has developed concentration problems in school that have been linked to a significant decline in grades. When interviewed, he explains that his mind is occupied with worrying about his mother, who has a serious autoimmune disease. As his grades falter, he becomes increasingly demoralized and sad, and he notices that his energy level drops, further compromising his ability to pay attention in school. At the same time, he complains of feeling restless and unable to sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of specific learning disorder.
Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood.
Separation anxiety disorder involving excessive worry about separation from mother.

correct_answer.text: Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood.

questions.explanation: The inattention seen in this boy relates to anxiety and depressive symptoms that are in reaction to his mother’s illness and his subsequent decline in grades. Inattention related to ADHD is not associated with worry and rumination, as would be the case in anxiety disorders.

questions.question_text: DSM5 outlines “with limited prosocial emotions” as a qualifier of conduct disorder. Which of the following characteristics supportive of this diagnosis involves disregard for and lack of concern about the feelings of others?
questions.explanation: Patients who demonstrate callous behavior and lack of empathy show disregard for and lack of concern about the feelings of others. Patients who are unconcerned about performance typically do not worry about problematic performance at school, work, or other activities and do not put forth effort to do well. Patients who show a lack of remorse or guilt do not feel bad when they do something wrong and show a general lack of concern about negative consequences of actions. Patients with shallow or deficient affect do not express feelings or show emotions to others, except in ways that seem shallow, insincere, or superficial. questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children?

options.text: The prevalence of ADHD in children is approximately 12-15% of the school-age population.
Approximately 15% of children are diagnosed with ADHD.
ADHD affects only 1% of the pediatric population.
The prevalence has remained constant at 0.5% despite increased screening.

questions.explanation: Population surveys suggest that ADHD occurs in most cultures in about 5% of children. Differences in ADHD prevalence rates across regions appear attributable mainly to different diagnostic and methodological practices. However, there also may be cultural variation in attitudes toward or interpretations of children’s behaviors. Clinical identification rates in the United States for African American and Latino populations tend to be lower than for 182 | Neurodevelopmental Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE Caucasian populations. Informant symptom ratings may be influenced by the cultural group of the child and the informant, suggesting that culturally appropriate practices are relevant in assessing ADHD.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes the risk and prognostic factors in intermittent explosive disorder (IED)?

options.text: First-degree relatives are at significantly lower risk for IED than the general population.
The etiology for the disorder is thought to be predominantly environmentally determined, and twin studies have not demonstrated a significant genetic influence for the impulsive aggression.

Patients with antisocial personality disorder or borderline personality disorder and those who have a prior diagnosis of disorders with disruptive behaviors (e.g., attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder) are at greater risk of comorbid IED.
IED typically has an acute onset and remits completely within a few months.
The prevalence in males versus females across cultures and studies is consistently about 4:1. Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders—QUESTIONS | 103

correct_answer.text: Patients with antisocial personality disorder or borderline personality disorder and those who have a prior diagnosis of disorders with disruptive behaviors (e.g., attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder) are at greater risk of comorbid IED.

questions.explanation: According to DSM-5, first-degree relatives of individuals with IED are at higher risk of also having the disorder, which has a strong genetic component to the impulsive aggression. The course typically is chronic and persistent, and the prevalence is greater in males than in females across some studies (odds ratios range from 1.4 to 2.3), although in other studies there is no gender difference. (In some cultures, the overall prevalence is lower.) Individuals with antisocial personality disorder or borderline personality disorder and those who have a history of disorders with disruptive behaviors (e.g., ADHD, conduct disorder, oppositional defiant disorder) are at greater risk of comorbid IED.

questions.question_text: By what age can a diagnosis of ASD be made reliably?

options.text: Autism can reliably be diagnosed at six months
Autism can reliably be diagnosed at nine months
Autism can reliable be diagnosed at 12 months
Autism can reliably be diagnosed by age two
Early diagnosis is futile since there are no interventions appropriate for children less than 4 years of age.

correct_answer.text: Autism can reliably be diagnosed by age two

questions.explanation: Many children demonstrate signs of autism as early as 12 months, and the disorder can reliably be diagnosed by 2 years of age. Early diagnosis can provide clarity to families. Early interventions are recommended because they offer optimal benefit for the child and his or her family, particularly because the brain is remarkably plastic in the first 3 years of life. Evidence suggests that integrated developmental and behavioral interventions can improve developmental quotients, functioning, and language skills in children who are 2 years old.

questions.explanation: Over-sexualized behaviour and unusual interest in genitals are specific behavioral signs listed for sexual abuse, whereas the other options are characteristic of physical abuse.

options.text: Constant hunger and poor personal hygiene

questions.question_text: According to Rutter's framework, which of the following is NOT listed as a mediator of parental psychiatric disorder's effect on a child?

options.text: Altered parenting capacity and interpersonal behaviour

questions.explanation: Rutter identifies three mediators: direct pernicious impact, indirect impact through altered parenting, and mediator variables such as social adversity and genetic/constitutional factors. School curriculum quality is not mentioned as a mediating mechanism in the source.

questions.explanation: A 2yearold child runs well, can go up and down stairs alone, can build a tower of 6 to 7 cubes, can draw a line, refers to himor herself by name, and can engage in parallel play. A 3yearold child can ride a tricycle, can build a tower of 9 or 10 cubes, can copy a circle, and is able to feed himor herself. questions.question_text: A mother with untreated depression presents with her 18-month-old toddler who shows passive non-compliance and reduced autonomy expression. Which of the following represents the MOST direct mediating mechanism between maternal depression and these toddler symptoms?

options.text: Altered parenting capacity and interpersonal behaviour

correct_answer.text: Altered parenting capacity and interpersonal behaviour

questions.explanation: The toddler's passive non-compliance and reduced autonomy are behavioural outcomes of altered parenting. Rutter's second mediator—indirect impact through altered interpersonal behaviour and parenting capacity—directly explains these observations. Genetic inheritance (A), social adversity (C), and constitutional factors (D) are distal mechanisms. Prenatal effects (E) would cause different outcomes.

questions.question_text: A child presenting with low self-esteem, sudden speech disorder, and self-mutilation most likely exhibits signs of which form of abuse?
questions.explanation: These signs—low self-esteem, sudden speech disorder, rocking, head-banging, and self-mutilation—are specifically listed as signs of possible emotional abuse.

questions.question_text: Which mediator variable proposed by Rutter would best explain why a child of a mentally ill parent develops psychopathology despite good parenting?
questions.explanation: If parenting is good but the child still develops disorder, genetic or constitutional factors (a mediator variable) would be the most plausible explanation, as it operates independently of parenting quality.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old girl with a history of sexual abuse at age 9 now presents with substance use, conduct problems, and depression. Which consequence of child sexual abuse does this clinical picture exemplify?

options.text: Non-specific risk factor for multiple forms of psychopathology
Suicidal ideation as the primary outcome

correct_answer.text: Non-specific risk factor for multiple forms of psychopathology

questions.explanation: That child maltreatment (including sexual abuse) is a non-specific risk factor for multiple forms of psychopathology, with increased rates of PTSD, depression, self-destructive behaviour, drug/alcohol problems, conduct/oppositional defiant disorder. Her multi-system presentation fits this description. Options A, C, D, and E are either too narrow or not supported by the comprehensive list provided.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which fails to qualify as a DSM-5 diagnostic criterion for language disorder?

options.text: Persistent difficulties in the acquisition and use of language across modalities due to impairment in comprehension or production.
Language abilities must be substantially lower than age-expected levels.
Symptom onset in the early developmental phase.
Difficulties cannot be attributed to hearing impairment or sensory limitations.
Failure to meet criteria for mixed receptive-expressive language disorder or a pervasive developmental disorder.

correct_answer.text: Failure to meet criteria for mixed receptive-expressive language disorder or a pervasive developmental disorder.

questions.explanation: Options A through D constitute the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for language disorder. This diagnosis replaced the DSM-IV diagnoses expressive language disorder and mixed receptive-expressive language disorder. Option E is a criterion for expressive language disorder in DSM-IV and is thus incorrect. In contrast to DSM-IV, in DSM-5 meeting criteria for pervasive developmental disorder does not preclude one from being diagnosed with language disorder.

questions.explanation: Anxiety disorders appear consistently as a consequence in both school-age children (affective, anxiety and conduct disorders) and adolescents (anxiety disorders, phobias, panic disorders). Other conditions are not present across all stages.

questions.question_text: A 20-month-old toddler is brought by his parents who are concerned about his development. They report that he rarely makes eye contact, does not respond when his name is called, has not started babbling, does not point to objects to share interest, and does not social smile. He shows repetitive motor behaviours and seems to underreact to sounds. He does not engage in imitative or imaginative play. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?

options.text: A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
A diagnosis of sterotypic movement disorder
A diagnosis of specific learning disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

questions.explanation: The toddler\'s presentation  reduced eye gaze, absent joint attention, failure to orient to name, absent social smile, delayed babbling, reduced imitation, repetitive motor behaviours, and sensory abnormalities — is characteristic of early autism spectrum disorder (ASD), making option A correct (DSM-5-TR p.160; Kaplan & Sadock p.2468). ADHD is characterised by inattention and hyperactivity without this social-communication profile. Stereotypic movement disorder involves repetitive purposeless motor behaviour but lacks the pervasive social-communication deficits seen here. Language disorder affects communication specifically but does not account for the social reciprocity, sensory, and motor features described. Specific learning disorder is not diagnosable in a toddler and does not fit this presentation.
